slides.narration: Welcome to week four of CPY 701, the first of two weeks on theoretical orientations. If weeks one to three told you who we are and where we sit, weeks four and five hand you the lenses through which counselors see a client. Today: three great families, the psychodynamic, the humanistic-experiential and the existential, from Freud's couch to Rogers's chair to Frankl's search for meaning. By the end you will explain each orientation's view of suffering, its engine of change, the counselor's stance and its signature techniques, and you will begin your first theory-informed case conceptualisation.

slides.narration: Four outcomes. One, explain the key concepts, goals and techniques of psychodynamic, person-centred, Gestalt and existential counseling. Two, evaluate the strengths, limitations and cultural fit of each orientation, including fit with Nigerian clients. Three, compare their assumptions about human nature side by side. Four, produce your first theory-informed case conceptualisation using a structured chain: data, lens, hypothesis, intervention, evaluation. Hold on to outcome four; it is the skill that all the others serve.

slides.title: Theory as a map, and the conceptualisation chain

items.lead: A theory is a map with a legend:
items.text: it tells you what to notice, what to ignore and what to do next, openly enough to be criticised.
counseling is conversation with good intentions; with only one theory, it is a recipe applied to people who never read the cookbook.
pluralism with coherence, several lenses held by one disciplined method.
gather data; choose a lens; hypothesise what maintains the suffering; select the intervention the hypothesis implies; evaluate whether help helped.
you meet this week and next is a different way of filling links two and three of that chain.

slides.narration: A theory is not a dogma; it is a map with a legend. It tells you what to notice, what to ignore and what to do next, and it declares its assumptions openly. Without theory, counseling becomes conversation with good intentions; with only one theory, it becomes a recipe applied to people who never read the cookbook. So we aim for pluralism with coherence: several lenses, one disciplined method. And here is the method, the conceptualisation chain you will use with every orientation: gather data; choose a lens; hypothesise what maintains the suffering; select the intervention the hypothesis implies; evaluate whether help helped. Five links. Every theory we meet this week and next is a different way of filling links two and three.

slides.title: Six branches; three we climb this week

cards.title: Psychodynamic
cards.text: Suffering as unconscious conflict and repeating relational patterns. THIS WEEK.

cards.title: Humanistic-experiential
cards.text: Suffering as blocked growth and disowned experience. THIS WEEK.

cards.title: Existential
cards.text: Suffering as confrontation with the givens of existence. THIS WEEK.

cards.title: Behavioural-cognitive
cards.text: Suffering as learned and thinking patterns. Week 5.

cards.title: Constructivist
cards.text: Suffering as story: narrative and solution-focused. Week 5.

cards.title: Systemic
cards.text: Suffering as relationship and context: family systems. Week 5.

slides.narration: Picture the family tree of counseling theories as six branches. This week we climb three. The psychodynamic branch: suffering as unconscious conflict and repeating relational patterns. The humanistic-experiential branch: suffering as blocked growth and disowned experience. The existential branch: suffering as confrontation with the givens of existence. Next week, three more: the behavioural-cognitive branch, suffering as learned and thinking patterns; the constructivist branch, suffering as story; and the systemic branch, suffering as relationship and context. Six branches, one tree: every branch attempts to explain how change happens. A mature counselor can name which branch they are standing on at any moment of a session.

slides.title: Core concepts: conflict, defence, transference

items.text: much of mental life is outside awareness, and nothing in the mind is accidental.
they protect against anxiety but distort reality and consume energy.
early relationships template adult ones.
the client replays old relational patterns with you; not interference, but the most valuable data in the room.
your side of the same dance; a diagnostic instrument once examined, a hazard while unexamined.
conflict, wish against fear, love against hate, loyalty against freedom.

slides.narration: Begin with psychodynamic thinking. Its claims: much of mental life is unconscious; psychic life is determined, so nothing in the mind is accidental; defences protect us from anxiety but distort reality and consume energy; early attachment and object relations template our adult relationships; and transference, the client replaying old relational patterns with you, is not interference but data, perhaps the most valuable data in the room. Countertransference, your side of the same dance, is a diagnostic instrument once examined and a hazard while unexamined. Suffering, in this lens, is conflict: wish against fear, love against hate, loyalty against freedom.

slides.title: The psychodynamic line of work

steps.title: Free association
steps.text: Say whatever comes; the seams of the mind show at the edges.

steps.title: Dreams & slips
steps.text: The unconscious speaks in compromise formations; listen for them.

steps.title: Resistance
steps.text: What the client avoids marks exactly where the work lives.

steps.title: Transference work
steps.text: The old pattern repeats live with you, and can be examined live.

steps.title: Working through
steps.text: Insight repeated until it becomes structure, not merely news.

slides.note: Goal: insight and structural change. Brief psychodynamic therapies compress this into 20-40 sessions around a core conflictual relationship theme.
slides.narration: The classical technique follows a line. Free association: say whatever comes, and the seams will show. Dream analysis and slips: the unconscious speaks in compromise formations, so listen for them. Interpretation of resistance: what the client avoids marks exactly where the work lives. Transference work: the old pattern repeats live with you, and therefore can be examined live. And working through: insight repeated until it becomes structure, not merely news. The goal is insight and structural change, making the unconscious conscious so that the self can govern what once governed it. Contemporary brief psychodynamic therapies compress this into twenty to forty sessions around a core conflictual relationship theme, and that brief form is the version most worth knowing for practice today.

slides.title: Psychodynamic: strengths, limits, cultural fit

items.text: depth of meaning; explains repetition; a genuine evidence base for brief dynamic therapy in depression and some anxiety presentations; a sophisticated theory of the relationship itself.
classical form is long and costly; concepts resist measurement; progress can be hard to demonstrate to clients, funders and courts.
an introspective, verbal, individual self; insight as virtue; candor as health. These are cultural positions, not universal facts.
whose meaning system defines insight here, and does the client share it?

callout.label: Practice note:
callout.text: brief psychodynamic work fits our settings far better than classical analysis; learn the brief form first.

slides.narration: Evaluate honestly. Strengths: depth, because it explains meaning and repetition, the patterns clients recognise but cannot stop; a genuine evidence base for brief dynamic therapy in depression and some anxiety presentations; and a sophisticated theory of the relationship itself. Limits: the classical form is long and costly; its concepts resist measurement; and progress can be hard to demonstrate to clients, funders and courts. Cultural assumptions: an introspective, verbal, individual self; insight as virtue; verbal candor as health. These are cultural positions, not universal facts. With Nigerian clients, ask before assuming: whose meaning system defines insight here, and does the client share it? In practice, the brief psychodynamic form fits our settings far better than classical analysis; learn the brief form first.

slides.quote: Where id was, there ego shall be.
slides.by: Sigmund Freud · the psychodynamic ambition in six words
slides.narration: Freud condensed the whole project into six words: where id was, there ego shall be. Not the elimination of desire and conflict, but the enlargement of the part of the self that can look at them, name them and choose. Every later orientation either inherited that ambition or rebelled against it, and the first great rebellion is our second family this week.

slides.title: Rogers: the conditions that carry change

items.text: the counselor is real and transparent within the relationship, not a mask.
prizing the person without making change the price of acceptance.
sensing the client's private world as if it were your own, without ever losing the as-if.
given these conditions, people move toward becoming; the client holds the map.
reflections that test your understanding moment by moment; the courage to stay non-directive when every fiber urges advice.

slides.narration: Now the rebellion that became its own tradition. Rogers reversed the authority: the client, not the expert, holds the map of their own experience. Change occurs when certain conditions persist, and three carry the practice. Congruence: the counselor is real and transparent within the relationship, not a mask. Unconditional positive regard: prizing the person without making change the price of acceptance. Empathic understanding: sensing the client's private world as if it were your own, without ever losing the as-if. The actualising tendency does the rest: given these conditions, people move toward becoming. And technique here is not a set of tricks but a discipline: reflections that test your understanding moment by moment, and the courage to remain non-directive when every fiber urges advice.

slides.title: What person-centred is, and is not

left.title: It is
items: Disciplined presence; every reflection a hypothesis offered for correction
A commitment to the client's authority over their own life
A measured, research-born tradition: our field's first process research

right.title: It is not
items: Permissiveness or the absence of method
Just listening while a client rambles
A refusal to influence; it is a refusal to replace the client's voice

slides.narration: Let us clear the caricature. Person-centred work is not permissiveness, not the absence of method, not just listening while a client rambles. It is disciplined presence: every reflection is a hypothesis offered for correction; every silence is chosen, not defaulted to; and the non-directiveness is a commitment to the client's authority over their own life, which is harder than directing. Nor is it naive: Rogers measured his conditions, invited observation and welcomed disconfirmation. The person-centred tradition gave our field its first rigorous process research and, eventually, the common-factors evidence base that every orientation now shares.

slides.title: Gestalt: awareness, experiment, ownership

items.text: awareness as the engine of change; the here-and-now as the only place experience exists; figure and ground; unfinished business; contact boundaries such as introjection, projection, retroflection and confluence.
the empty chair for dialogue with a person or a part; exaggeration of a gesture to hear its message; staying with the feeling rather than talking about it; dream work as lived scene.
integration and ownership; the client moves from it happens to me, to I do this.
experiments require consent, pacing and cultural care where emotional display is disciplined by norm.

slides.narration: Gestalt therapy radicalises presence into experiment. Its concepts: awareness as the engine of change; the here-and-now as the only place experience exists; figure and ground, what emerges as urgent against the background of the field; unfinished business, unexpressed feeling that organises present contact; and contact boundaries, the styles by which we interrupt meeting. Its techniques are experiments, not prescriptions: the empty chair for dialogue with a person or a part; exaggeration of a gesture to hear its message; staying with the feeling rather than talking about it; dream work as lived scene. The goal is integration and ownership: the client moves from it happens to me, to I do this. It demands consent, pacing and cultural care.

slides.title: The givens of existence and the courage to face them

items.text: death; freedom and its responsibility; existential isolation; and the possibility of meaninglessness.
not always a symptom to remove; sometimes an accurate perception of the human condition.
phenomenological and Socratic exploration of how this person lives their givens: where they flee freedom, deny limits, or lose meaning.
the will to meaning and tragic optimism; even in unchangeable suffering, a stance can be chosen.
authenticity, responsibility, and a meaning the client can carry.

slides.narration: The existential orientation begins not from pathology but from the givens of existence: death; freedom and its responsibility; existential isolation; and the possibility of meaninglessness. Yalom's point: psychopathology often arises from collision with these givens, so anxiety is sometimes not a symptom to remove but an accurate perception of the human condition. The counselor's work is phenomenological and Socratic: explore how this person lives their givens, where they flee freedom or deny limits. Frankl's logotherapy adds the will to meaning and tragic optimism: even in unchangeable suffering, a stance can be chosen. The goals are authenticity, responsibility, and a meaning the client can carry.

slides.title: Four orientations side by side
rows: Accurate reflection of feeling and meaning
Collision with the givens of existence
slides.note: Each row also carries cultural assumptions; evaluate them, do not swallow them.
slides.narration: Set the four orientations of this week side by side and the differences become crisp. Psychodynamic: suffering as unconscious conflict; change through insight and the working through of transference; the counselor as interpreter of the repeating pattern; signature moves of free association and interpretation. Person-centred: suffering as blocked growth; change through the core conditions; the counselor as real, prizing, empathic companion; signature move of accurate reflection. Gestalt: suffering as interrupted awareness; change through experiment in the here-and-now; the counselor as active director of experiments; signature move of the empty chair. Existential: suffering as collision with the givens; change through courageous facing and meaning-making; the counselor as fellow traveller and questioner; signature move of Socratic exploration. Each row also carries cultural assumptions; evaluate them, do not swallow them.

slides.title: Whose culture is inside these theories?

items.text: assumes an introspective, verbal, individual self; insight as the prize.
self-direction can collide with hierarchical and communal expectations, yet warmth, prizing and empathy travel astonishingly well.
expressive experiments meet norms that discipline public feeling; consent and pacing become ethical necessities.
framed in a secular idiom, yet its questions of meaning, death and responsibility resonate with religious and communal worldviews, including African personhood-in-community.
test imported theory locally, adapt with transparency, and report what you learn.

slides.narration: Now the question week two trained you to ask: whose culture is inside these theories? Psychodynamic thinking assumes an introspective, verbal, individual self, with insight as the prize. Person-centred assumptions of self-direction can collide with hierarchical and communal expectations, yet its conditions of warmth, prizing and empathy travel astonishingly well across cultures. Gestalt's expressive experiments meet norms that discipline public feeling, so consent and pacing become ethical necessities, not stylistic choices. Existentialism is framed in a secular idiom, yet its questions of meaning, death and responsibility resonate deeply with religious and communal worldviews, including African philosophies of personhood-in-community. The standing rule from week two holds: test imported theory locally, adapt with transparency, and report what you learn.

slides.title: Week 4 in review
items: Four orientations, four answers to why this person suffers and how change happens.
Psychodynamic: unconscious conflict, insight and the transference; person-centred: blocked growth and the core conditions.
Gestalt: interrupted awareness and present experiment; existential: the givens and courageous meaning-making.
Each orientation carries a counselor stance, a signature technique, and cultural assumptions to evaluate.
Above them all sits the conceptualisation chain: data, lens, hypothesis, intervention, evaluation.
slides.narration: Gather the week. Four orientations, four answers to the questions why does this person suffer and how does change happen: unconscious conflict and insight; blocked growth and the core conditions; interrupted awareness and present experiment; collision with the givens and courageous meaning-making. Each carries a stance for the counselor and a signature technique, and each carries cultural assumptions to be evaluated rather than swallowed. And above them all sits the chain that holds your practice together whatever the lens: data, lens, hypothesis, intervention, evaluation.
